title: Effect of Temperature on Rate
content:
# Effect of Temperature on Rate

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Describe how temperature affects reaction rate
- Explain the effect using collision theory and energy distribution
- Interpret Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curves
- Design experiments to investigate temperature effects

## Introduction

Temperature has a dramatic effect on reaction rate. A small increase in temperature can cause a large increase in rate. This is why we refrigerate food (to slow decomposition) and cook food at high temperatures (to speed up chemical changes).

## Key Concepts

### The Effect

**Increasing temperature increases the rate of reaction.**

**Rule of thumb:** For every 10°C rise in temperature, the rate approximately doubles.

This is a much larger effect than concentration - temperature has a dramatic impact on rate.

### Collision Theory Explanation

**Two reasons why higher temperature increases rate:**

**Reason 1: More frequent collisions**
- Higher temperature = particles have more kinetic energy
- Particles move faster
- More collisions occur per second
- (This is a minor effect)

**Reason 2: More energetic collisions (main reason)**
- At higher temperature, particles collide with more energy
- A greater proportion of collisions have energy ≥ activation energy
- More collisions are successful
- This is the major reason for the large effect

### Maxwell-Boltzmann Distribution

The **Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution** shows how particle energies are distributed in a sample.

[DIAGRAM: Maxwell-Boltzmann curves at two temperatures (T1 and T2 where T2 > T1) with activation energy marked]

```
Number of 
particles
    ↑
    |  /\  T₁ (lower temp)
    | /  \
    |/    \    /\  T₂ (higher temp)
    |      \  /  \
    |       \/    \
    |        \     \____
    |         \________\_____
    |________________________________→
              Energy      ↑Eₐ
```

**Key features:**
- Most particles have intermediate energies
- Few particles have very low or very high energies
- The area under the curve to the right of Eₐ = particles that can react
- At higher temperature, the curve shifts right and flattens
- Much larger area beyond Eₐ at higher temperature

### Why Temperature Has Such a Large Effect

**At lower temperature:**
- Small fraction of particles have energy ≥ Eₐ
- Few successful collisions

**At higher temperature:**
- Much larger fraction have energy ≥ Eₐ
- Many more successful collisions

The increase in successful collisions is much greater than the increase in collision frequency.

### Effect on Graphs

**Volume vs time at different temperatures:**

```
Volume (cm³)
    ↑
    |          High temp ___________
    |         /
    |       /   Medium temp ___________
    |     /    /
    |   /    /   Low temp ___________
    | /    /    /
    |/___/____/________________________→
                    Time (s)
```

**Observations:**
- Higher temperature = steeper initial gradient
- All reach same final volume (same amount of reactant)
- Higher temperature finishes faster

### Investigating Temperature - Sodium Thiosulfate

**Reaction:**
$$\text{Na}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3 + \text{2HCl} \rightarrow \text{2NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{SO}_2 + \text{S}$$

**Method:**
1. Heat sodium thiosulfate solution to required temperature
2. Place flask on paper with cross
3. Add acid (at same temperature) and start timer
4. Record time for cross to disappear
5. Repeat at different temperatures (e.g., 20°C, 30°C, 40°C, 50°C)
6. Keep concentrations and volumes constant

**Results:**

| Temperature (°C) | Time (s) | 1/time (s⁻¹) |
|------------------|----------|---------------|
| 20 | 120 | 0.0083 |
| 30 | 60 | 0.017 |
| 40 | 30 | 0.033 |
| 50 | 15 | 0.067 |

**Analysis:**
- Each 10°C increase approximately halves the time
- Rate (∝ 1/time) approximately doubles for each 10°C

### Practical Considerations

**Controlling temperature:**
- Use a water bath for accurate temperature control
- Pre-heat solutions before mixing
- Allow time for temperature to stabilize
- Measure temperature at start of reaction

**Keeping temperature constant:**
- Difficult for exothermic reactions (they heat up)
- Use large volumes or water bath to minimize temperature change

## Worked Examples

**Example 1:** Use collision theory to explain why a 10°C temperature increase approximately doubles the reaction rate.

**Solution:**
- At higher temperature, particles have more kinetic energy
- They move faster, so there are more collisions per second (minor effect)
- More importantly, collisions are more energetic
- Looking at the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, a small temperature increase shifts the curve significantly to the right
- The area beyond Eₐ (particles with enough energy to react) roughly doubles
- This means the proportion of successful collisions roughly doubles
- Therefore the rate approximately doubles

---

**Example 2:** Use the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution to explain why catalysts increase rate.

**Solution:**
- A catalyst lowers the activation energy (Eₐ)
- On the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve, this moves the Eₐ line to the left
- A larger area of the curve is now to the right of Eₐ
- More particles have sufficient energy to react
- More collisions are successful
- Rate increases
- (Note: the curve itself doesn't change - only where Eₐ is)

---

**Example 3:** A reaction takes 80 seconds at 25°C. Estimate how long it would take at 35°C.

**Solution:**
- Temperature increases by 10°C
- Rate approximately doubles
- If rate doubles, time halves
- Time ≈ 80 ÷ 2 = **40 seconds**

---

**Example 4:** At 20°C, a reaction has rate 0.5 mol/s. Estimate the rate at 40°C.

**Solution:**
- Temperature increases by 20°C (two lots of 10°C)
- Rate doubles twice: × 2 × 2 = × 4
- Rate at 40°C ≈ 0.5 × 4 = **2 mol/s**

## Common Mistakes

- **Mistake:** Saying particles gain kinetic energy and collide more often (incomplete)
- **Correct:** The main reason is more energetic collisions, not just more frequent ones

- **Mistake:** Drawing Maxwell-Boltzmann curves that cross at the peak
- **Correct:** Higher temperature curve is lower and broader (flattened)

- **Mistake:** Forgetting to pre-heat both solutions
- **Correct:** Both reactant solutions should be at the test temperature

## Practice Questions

1. State two reasons why increasing temperature increases reaction rate. Which has the greater effect? (4 marks)

2. Draw Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curves for the same substance at two different temperatures. Label the curves and the activation energy. (4 marks)

3. Use the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution to explain why temperature has such a large effect on reaction rate. (4 marks)

4. A reaction takes 200 seconds at 10°C. Estimate how long it would take at:
   a) 20°C (1 mark)
   b) 30°C (1 mark)
   c) 40°C (1 mark)

5. Describe how you would investigate the effect of temperature on the rate of reaction between sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid. (6 marks)

6. Explain why food lasts longer in a refrigerator than at room temperature. (3 marks)

## Key Terms Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution | A graph showing how particle energies are distributed |
| Kinetic energy | The energy of movement |
| Activation energy | The minimum energy needed for a successful collision |
| Water bath | A container of water used to control temperature |

## Summary

- **Temperature increase → rate increase** (dramatic effect)
- **10°C rise ≈ doubles the rate**
- Two reasons:
  1. Particles move faster (more collisions) - minor effect
  2. Collisions more energetic (more exceed Eₐ) - major effect
- **Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution** explains why:
  - Higher T shifts curve right
  - Much larger area beyond Eₐ
  - Many more particles can react
- Practical: use water bath, pre-heat solutions, control variables
